categories.name: Access Control
categories.note: No authentication or authorization anywhere. All pages, all CRUD and the Blazor hub are reachable anonymously. Acknowledged as out of scope in the project's SECURITY.md, but it remains the dominant risk.

categories.name: Injection
categories.note: EF Core LINQ throughout; zero raw-SQL APIs. All 7 SQL-shaped matches are documentation strings in D4DemoService.cs, not executed statements.

categories.name: Cross-Site Scripting
categories.note: Zero MarkupString/Html.Raw sinks. CSP now uses a per-request nonce with no unsafe-inline or unsafe-eval for scripts.

categories.name: Security Misconfiguration
categories.note: Strong header baseline. Open host filter, unauthenticated /health, no .gitignore, and a CSP that allows unused origins.

categories.name: Cryptographic Failures
categories.note: No HTTPS listener is configured at all, so HTTPS redirection and HSTS are inert. Customer PII is plaintext at rest.

categories.name: Input Validation
categories.note: SecurityGuard.Validate enforces schema-derived DataAnnotations at the service boundary on customer, order and stock writes. One write path bypasses it.

categories.name: Logging & Audit
categories.note: Structured AUDIT entries on 12 mutation sites, but the actor is always 'anonymous', so the trail cannot attribute an action to a person.

categories.name: Vulnerable & Outdated Components
categories.note: Verified clean: `dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive` reports no vulnerable packages against nuget.org today. A scan script exists but is not wired into CI.

strengths.title: No SQL injection surface
strengths.detail: EF Core LINQ exclusively. Zero FromSqlRaw / ExecuteSqlRaw / SqlCommand / CommandText across 58 C# files. LIKE searches use EF.Functions.Like with a parameterized pattern. The 7 matches for concatenated-SQL patterns are all help text in D4DemoService.cs describing the legacy 4GL, not executed SQL.

strengths.title: No XSS sinks
strengths.detail: Zero MarkupString, Html.Raw or equivalent. Blazor's automatic contextual encoding is intact on every render path.

strengths.title: CSP hardened with a per-request nonce
strengths.detail: script-src is 'self' plus a cryptographically random per-request nonce generated with RandomNumberGenerator; unsafe-eval and script unsafe-inline are both gone, and _Layout.cshtml stamps the nonce on all three script tags. style-src retains unsafe-inline only because MudBlazor injects styles at runtime - the materially lower-risk directive.

strengths.title: Deprecated X-XSS-Protection correctly removed
strengths.detail: The header is absent and the code documents why, deferring to CSP as the modern control.

strengths.title: Full security header baseline
strengths.detail: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN, Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin, and a restrictive Permissions-Policy on every response.

strengths.title: Server-side validation at the service boundary
strengths.detail: SecurityGuard.Validate runs DataAnnotations on CustomerDto, OrderDto and StockDto inside the service layer rather than only in the UI, so invalid input is rejected regardless of what the client sends. Limits mirror the real stores7 column widths.

strengths.title: Structured audit logging on mutations
strengths.detail: SecurityGuard.Audit emits a greppable AUDIT actor/action/entity/key/timestamp record at 12 create, update and delete sites.

strengths.title: No hard-coded secrets
strengths.detail: No credentials, keys or tokens in source or configuration. Security:DatabasePassword is an empty config seam, and the code explicitly directs the real key to user-secrets or Key Vault.

strengths.title: Rate limiting and antiforgery configured
strengths.detail: A partitioned fixed-window global limiter (1000/min) with a 429 rejection code, plus AddAntiforgery/UseAntiforgery in the pipeline.

strengths.title: Detailed errors gated to Development
strengths.detail: Blazor DetailedErrors is bound to IsDevelopment(), and UseExceptionHandler("/Error") plus UseHsts apply only outside Development.

strengths.title: Seed file I/O uses fixed server paths
strengths.detail: DataSeeder builds paths from AppContext.BaseDirectory with internal constant filenames. No user input reaches the filesystem - no traversal exposure.

strengths.title: Dependencies verified clean
strengths.detail: All 9 direct packages plus transitives checked against nuget.org during this audit: no vulnerable packages reported.

findings.title: No authentication or authorization anywhere in the application
findings.evidence: Zero [Authorize] attributes across 73 source files. Zero AddAuthentication, AddAuthorization, UseAuthentication or UseAuthorization calls in Program.cs. MapBlazorHub() is mapped with no RequireAuthorization(). Combined with the Kestrel binding to 0.0.0.0:5000 (see S-3), every page and every mutation is reachable by anyone who can route to the host.
findings.risk: Any anonymous visitor can read every customer, order and stock record, create and delete them, and open a SignalR circuit to invoke server-side component logic directly. There is no control anywhere in the request path that would stop them.

remediation.summary: Register an identity provider and apply a global default-deny authorization policy, so every page requires sign-in without editing any page.
steps: Add ASP.NET Core Identity or the organisation's OIDC provider: AddAuthentication().AddOpenIdConnect(...) plus AddAuthorization().
Call UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() after UseRouting() and before UseAntiforgery().

Set a global fallback policy - AddAuthorizationBuilder().SetFallbackPolicy(new AuthorizationPolicyBuilder().RequireAuthenticatedUser().Build()) - so pages added later are protected by default rather than by memory.
Mark the sign-in and error endpoints [AllowAnonymous]; decide explicitly whether /health stays anonymous (see S-7).
Protect the circuit: app.MapBlazorHub().RequireAuthorization().

findings.verification: An unauthenticated GET /customers returns 302 to the sign-in endpoint. After signing in, /customers renders exactly as it does today. dotnet build reports 0 errors and the seeded data still displays.

findings.title: Destructive operations carry no authorization check of their own

locations.excerpt: public async Task<bool> delete_customerAsync(int customerNum, CancellationToken ct = default)
public async Task<bool> delete_orderAsync(int orderNum, CancellationToken ct = default)
public async Task<bool> delete_stockAsync(CancellationToken ct = default)

findings.evidence: The three delete methods and the six update/add methods perform no role or permission check. They rely entirely on the UI to decide who may call them. Adding authentication (S-1) makes them require a signed-in user, but every signed-in user would still be able to delete any record.
findings.risk: Once authentication is added, any authenticated account - including a read-only or low-privilege one - can still destroy customer, order and stock records. Read access and write access should not be the same privilege.

remediation.summary: Introduce a CanModify policy and require it on the write paths, leaving reads broad.
steps: Depends on S-1: an identity must exist before a role can be checked.
Add a CanModify policy (AddAuthorizationBuilder().AddPolicy("CanModify", p => p.RequireRole("Editor", "Admin"))).

Enforce it at the service boundary rather than only on the component, so an alternative call path cannot bypass it - SecurityGuard is the natural place, alongside the existing Validate and Audit calls.
Keep read methods unrestricted beyond authentication, preserving today's behaviour for viewers.

findings.verification: A user in a read-only role can open /customers and see records, but a delete returns a 403 and writes no audit entry; a user in the Editor role deletes successfully and the AUDIT line appears in the log.

findings.title: No HTTPS listener is configured - the app serves plaintext HTTP on all interfaces
findings.evidence: The only Kestrel endpoint declared anywhere is plaintext HTTP bound to 0.0.0.0:5000 (all interfaces). No HTTPS endpoint, no certificate configuration and no https:// URL exists in any configuration file. UseHttpsRedirection() and UseHsts() are both present but cannot function: with no HTTPS port to redirect to, ASP.NET Core logs 'Failed to determine the https port for redirect' and passes the request through in cleartext, and the HSTS header is only ever emitted over HTTPS.
findings.risk: All traffic - customer names, addresses, phone numbers, order data, and any session cookie added by S-1 - crosses the network in cleartext and can be read or modified by anyone on the path. This finding is easy to miss because the codebase *looks* correctly configured: the two protective middlewares are present, and only the absent listener makes them inert.

remediation.summary: Terminate TLS - either configure an HTTPS endpoint on Kestrel or front the app with a proxy that does - and bind HTTP to loopback only.
steps: Preferred in production: terminate TLS at a reverse proxy or ingress, bind Kestrel to 127.0.0.1 rather than 0.0.0.0, and add UseForwardedHeaders so the app sees the original scheme.
Otherwise configure an HTTPS endpoint directly with a real certificate (Kestrel:Endpoints:Https:Url plus a Certificate section referencing the store or a PFX path from a secret store).
Once an HTTPS endpoint exists, UseHttpsRedirection() and UseHsts() start working with no code change.
Do not leave 0.0.0.0 bound to plaintext HTTP on any networked host.

findings.verification: curl -I http://<host>:5000/ returns 307/301 to https://, and the HTTPS response carries Strict-Transport-Security. The startup log no longer contains 'Failed to determine the https port for redirect'.

findings.title: Host header filtering disabled (AllowedHosts: "*")
findings.evidence: The wildcard disables ASP.NET Core's host filtering middleware, so the application answers to any Host header value.
findings.risk: Enables host-header attacks: poisoned absolute URLs in generated links and emails, cache poisoning where a shared cache is in front, and easier routing of the app through an attacker-controlled domain. The impact is limited today because no password-reset or email flow builds absolute URLs, but that changes the moment S-1 adds one.

remediation.summary: Set AllowedHosts to the hostnames the application is actually served on.
steps: Replace the wildcard with a semicolon-separated list of real hostnames.
Keep "*" only in appsettings.Development.json if local tooling needs it.

findings.verification: A request carrying Host: evil.example.com returns 400 Bad Request; a request with the real host serves the app normally.

findings.title: Customer PII is stored unencrypted at rest
findings.evidence: The encryption seam added by the previous remediation pass (Security:DatabasePassword, applied to the SQLite connection in Program.cs) is present but empty, so it is inactive. stores7.db and the SeedData/*.unl files therefore hold customer names, street addresses and phone numbers in plaintext on disk. Program.cs documents that enabling it also requires swapping to a SQLCipher-capable SQLite bundle and re-creating the database.
findings.risk: Any read access to the filesystem - a stolen backup, a misconfigured volume mount, or a path-traversal flaw elsewhere - yields the full customer table with no further effort. The seed files are equally readable and travel with the repository.

remediation.summary: Activate the existing encryption seam, or host the database on an encrypted volume. The seam is already wired - only the provider swap and a key remain.
steps: Swap SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlite3 for SQLitePCLRaw.bundle_e_sqlcipher in the csproj.
Supply Security:DatabasePassword from user-secrets in development and Key Vault or equivalent in production - never from appsettings.json.
Re-create the database so it is written encrypted; an existing plaintext file is not encrypted in place by setting a password.
Simpler alternative with no code change at all: keep the plaintext file but host it on an encrypted volume, and treat the seed .unl files as sensitive.
Prefer either of the above over column-level encryption, which would break sorting and filtering on the affected columns.

findings.verification: The .db file is not readable as plaintext with a hex viewer or the sqlite3 CLI without the key, while the application opens it with the key and every page behaves as before.

findings.title: One write path bypasses both input validation and audit logging

locations.excerpt: public async Task<bool> InsertItemsForOrderAsync(int orderNum, List<OrderItemDto> items, CancellationToken ct = default)

findings.evidence: InsertItemsForOrderAsync persists order line items - including StockNum, Quantity and TotalPrice - with no SecurityGuard.Validate call on the incoming OrderItemDto list and no SecurityGuard.Audit entry. Every other persisting method in the three write services calls both. The plain LogInformation that is present records a count, not an auditable action record. This is a gap in the coverage the project's own SECURITY.md claims for S-5 and S-8.
findings.risk: Order line items - the financially significant records - can be written with values that bypass the DataAnnotations enforced everywhere else, and their creation leaves no entry in the audit trail. The inconsistency is the real problem: a control applied at 12 of 13 sites reads as complete during review.

remediation.summary: Call SecurityGuard.Validate on each item and SecurityGuard.Audit after the save, matching the pattern used by the other twelve write sites.
steps: Add DataAnnotations to OrderItemDto mirroring the items table column definitions, as CustomerDto/OrderDto/StockDto already do.
Validate each item before it is added to the context.
Emit an audit record after SaveChangesAsync, keyed on the order number.
Then re-check coverage mechanically rather than by eye: every SaveChangesAsync in the service layer should have an adjacent Audit call.

findings.verification: Submitting an order line with an over-length ManuCode is rejected with a validation message; a valid submission saves as before and produces an `AUDIT ... action=CREATE entity=items` line in logs/informix-demo-3-*.log.

findings.title: Health endpoint is exposed without authentication
findings.evidence: /health is mapped with no authorization and includes a DbContext check, so an anonymous caller learns whether the application and its database are reachable.
findings.risk: Minor reconnaissance value: confirms the technology and whether the database is up, and gives an unauthenticated endpoint that can be polled. Low on its own; it matters slightly more while S-1 leaves everything else anonymous too.

remediation.summary: Decide deliberately: keep a minimal anonymous liveness probe, and put the detailed readiness check behind authentication or an internal-only port.
steps: Expose an anonymous liveness endpoint that returns no detail (a predicate that selects no checks).
Map the detailed readiness endpoint separately and require authorization, or bind it to an internal management port.
If an orchestrator probes /health, confirm it still receives 200 before deploying.

findings.verification: Anonymous GET /health returns 200 with no component detail; anonymous GET /health/ready returns 401; the orchestrator's probe still passes.

findings.title: Audit trail cannot attribute actions to a person
findings.owasp: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.evidence: The actor field is the hard-coded literal "anonymous" on every audit record, because no identity exists to record. The code documents this and marks it as the single place to change once authentication lands.
findings.risk: The audit trail proves that a record changed and when, but never who changed it. For incident response and dispute resolution - the two reasons to keep an audit trail - that is most of the value missing. This is a consequence of S-1 rather than a defect in the audit implementation, which is otherwise well built.

remediation.summary: Once S-1 supplies an identity, read the authenticated user in SecurityGuard.Audit. The change is a single line.
steps: Depends on S-1.
Inject IHttpContextAccessor into the audit path and record User.Identity.Name, falling back to "anonymous" only when genuinely unauthenticated.
Consider also recording the client IP and a correlation id so an audit line can be tied to a request.
Ship audit records to a store the application itself cannot rewrite.

findings.verification: A delete performed by a signed-in user produces an AUDIT line naming that user, not "anonymous".

findings.title: No .gitignore - the PII database and log directory can be committed

locations.excerpt: no .gitignore present; stores7.db, stores7.db-wal, stores7.db-shm and logs/ sit in the project root

findings.evidence: The project root contains no .gitignore. stores7.db (customer PII), its WAL and shared-memory files, and the logs/ directory are all in the tree and would be captured by a `git add .`.
findings.risk: A committed database publishes the customer table to everyone with repository access, and it stays in git history after deletion. Log files can carry the same data. The audit and validation work is undermined if the data itself ships with the source.

remediation.summary: Add a .gitignore covering build output, the database, logs and local secrets.
steps: Add the standard .NET ignores (bin/, obj/) plus *.db, *.db-wal, *.db-shm, logs/ and .env.
If the repository already contains any of these, remove them from tracking with `git rm --cached` - and if the database was ever pushed, treat the data as disclosed.
Keep the SeedData/*.unl files if they are demo data, but confirm they contain no real customer records.

findings.verification: `git status --porcelain` shows no database or log files as untracked additions after a clean build and a run of the app.

findings.title: Dependency scan exists but is not enforced in CI

locations.excerpt: # S-9 - Dependency vulnerability scan. ... Wire this into CI so dependency risk is checked continuously, not just once.

findings.evidence: scan-vulnerable.ps1 correctly runs `dotnet list package --vulnerable --include-transitive` and exits non-zero on High/Critical. No CI workflow was found in the audited tree that invokes it, and the script's own header notes it still needs wiring in. Run during this audit, it reports no vulnerable packages, so the current position is genuinely clean.
findings.risk: A point-in-time clean result goes stale: an advisory published tomorrow against MudBlazor, EF Core or QuestPDF would not surface until someone remembers to run the script manually.

remediation.summary: Invoke the existing script from CI on every build, and enable automated upgrade PRs.
steps: Add a CI step that runs scan-vulnerable.ps1 and fails the build on its non-zero exit.
Enable Dependabot or Renovate so upgrades are proposed automatically rather than discovered during an audit.
Note the script's matching is text-based ('high'/'critical' anywhere in the output); prefer parsing the JSON output if the CI gate needs to be precise.
remediation.codeAfter:
- name: Dependency vulnerability scan
  shell: pwsh
  run: ./scan-vulnerable.ps1

findings.verification: The CI step runs on every build and is green; pinning a known-vulnerable package version turns it red.

findings.title: CSP permits external font origins the application never uses
findings.evidence: The policy allows fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com, but no markup, stylesheet or configuration in the project references either origin - MudBlazor's CSS and fonts are served from _content/MudBlazor locally.
findings.risk: No direct exploitability. It is a slightly wider policy than needed, and unused allowances tend to outlive the reason they were added. Removing them tightens the policy at zero cost.

remediation.summary: Drop the two Google Fonts origins from style-src and font-src.
steps: Remove https://fonts.googleapis.com from style-src and https://fonts.gstatic.com from font-src.
Load the page and confirm no CSP violations and no fallback fonts - if a font does fail, the correct fix is to self-host it rather than restore the allowance.

findings.verification: The application renders identically and the browser console reports no CSP violations across all five routes.

roadmap.name: Transport and access control
roadmap.rationale: The two changes that actually alter this application's exposure. S-3 is a configuration fix measured in minutes and should not wait for S-1: today every byte crosses the network in cleartext. S-1 then closes anonymous access, and S-2 separates read from write once identities exist.

roadmap.name: Configuration hardening
roadmap.rationale: Hours of work, no behaviour change. All four are settings or a new file; none touches application logic.

roadmap.name: Data protection and coverage gaps
roadmap.rationale: S-6 is a small, contained fix that restores the consistency the previous remediation pass intended. S-5 needs a provider swap and a database rebuild, so it is scheduled rather than squeezed in.

roadmap.name: Operational
roadmap.rationale: S-8 becomes a one-line change once S-1 lands. S-10 turns a point-in-time clean dependency result into a continuous one.

limitations: Static analysis only. The application was not built, deployed or exercised at runtime, so no finding here reflects observed behaviour. S-3 in particular is inferred from configuration; confirm it by checking the startup log for the 'Failed to determine the https port for redirect' warning.
The Informix 4GL source was not audited in this run, so 'legacy-inherited' versus 'migration-introduced' classification is inferred from the generated code and its comments alone.

Deployment context was assumed, not verified. If this application is only ever run on a developer's loopback interface, the exposure ratings for S-1, S-3 and S-4 are lower than stated; if it is reachable from a network, they are correct as written. The Kestrel binding to 0.0.0.0 is what makes the internet-facing reading the safer default.

Infrastructure, network policy, reverse-proxy configuration and any WAF in front of the application were out of scope. A proxy terminating TLS would change S-3 materially - that is worth confirming before acting on it.
Business-logic correctness was assessed only where intent was inferable from the code. Domain rules such as pricing authority, credit limits and valid order state transitions were not verified.
The dependency result is a point-in-time check against nuget.org on the scan date and says nothing about advisories published afterwards.
bin/ and obj/ build output were excluded from findings analysis; they were used only for the dependency restore.
